pairings.thesis: Primary. Leadership-change headlines get priced as drama; planned, internal successions don't deliver it. Sell premium on low-JEV filings; compare against high-JEV filings and ordinary days.
pairings.notes: In-sample n=150, edge=-0.53% NOT SUPPORTED. All 150 events are low-JEV (0.0 or 0.33). Top: PLTR CAO appt +8.4%, UNH CFO->advisor +7.7%, UBER GC transition +6.9%, INTC Products CEO resign +6.2%, NFLX Hastings transition +5.2%. Bottom: UNH Optum CEO appt -16.3%, ORCL Catz exit -15.1%, CRM Pres+CFO appt -12.1%, BA Calhoun resign -9.3%, SBUX CFO depart -9.2%. High variance: routine appointments mix planned promotions (positive) with abrupt exits labeled low-JEV (negative). No high-JEV events to compare. Thesis not supported for cash-secured put on all low-JEV leadership changes.

pairings.thesis: 'CEO change' gets priced as drama. Planned successions (KO Quincey -> Braun) don't deliver it.
Secondary. A surprise exit has uncertain direction; the market may under-price the downside. Mirror image of the low-JEV pairings.
Mostly orderly promotions, so the post-filing implied move overstates what follows. Massive's CFO example is null overall; a JEV split showing a hidden effect is the story.
Stretch. A material exit is an event you hold through; the put may be cheap relative to the downside. High-JEV first announcements vs low-JEV recasts (KO June filing).
Abrupt or disputed resignations matter; most are retirements, so few events survive the split.
Direction is ambiguous; KO's examples were reporting recasts, not news. JEV does not score direction.
Massive's novelty floor ('guidance up, buy a call'). JEV adds nothing unless it also scores direction; guidance updates include cuts.
Earnings premium is overpriced, but obvious, boilerplate text (JEV adds nothing) and the post-filing entry misses the vol crush. Run last: largest event count.
